b: On November fifth, Ottawa tabled Budget twenty twenty-six, titled Masters of our destiny. What is in it for Alberta, and for Calgary? Here is a quick look.

First, the big picture. The deficit this year is sixty-two point three billion dollars, and about two hundred and eighty-nine billion over five years. The biggest new measure is the Productivity Mega Deduction: businesses can write off new machinery and equipment right away. It is worth about thirty-six billion dollars over five years.

We searched the whole budget, about two hundred and twenty thousand words. Alberta is named thirty-four times. Calgary, just twice. Edmonton, five times. For comparison, Québec is named seventy-four times, Ontario sixty-seven, and British Columbia forty-one.

Three of the twenty-eight nation-building projects sent to the federal Major Projects Office are in Alberta. The biggest is Pacific Link: a twelve hundred and fifty kilometre oil pipeline from Bruderheim to the coast near Delta, British Columbia. It would carry one million barrels a day, with at least ten percent offered to Indigenous owners.
Next to it is Pathways, large-scale carbon capture in the oil sands. With the Oil Sands Alliance's other commitments, it aims to cut sixteen million tonnes of emissions a year.
The third is Alberta High-Speed Rail. The budget lists it by name, with no dollar figure yet.

Alberta-based De Havilland gets up to two point five billion dollars in financing to build more waterbombers in Wheatland County, to fight wildfires in Canada and Europe. On defence, the budget names fighter facilities at CFB Cold Lake, a laboratory at CFB Suffield, and repairs across Alberta's bases.

Now, Calgary's two mentions. In August, Ottawa launched the Quantum Defence Innovation Secure Hub in Calgary, bringing quantum, defence and technology organisations together. And the Silver Springs Community Centre expansion is one of the projects named for the new Build Communities Strong Fund.

For households, there is a one-time Groceries and Essentials Benefit supplement in early twenty twenty-seven, for more than twelve million people on low and modest incomes. And Alberta's federal health and social transfers rise to about nine point two billion dollars this year, roughly eighteen hundred dollars per person.
Every passage that names Alberta is on the Federal Budget page. Calgary Data Desk, by Hassan Ali.
